Sunday, 9 pm
Badminton with Rekha again this morning. Week fourteen, I counted. It started because the court downstairs needed two players and we both happened to be standing there with rackets in April.
Now it's a thing. Sunday, 7 am, then chai on the bench. Today she told me about her dad's surgery and I told her about the job I didn't get. We weren't trying to be deep. It just came out between games.
I used to think I needed a big group and loads of invites. I have maybe three people now: Rekha, Deepa from work, and Anu on the phone every Wednesday. It's enough. More than enough.
Note to self, Simran: don't skip next Sunday, even if it rains. Rain just means chai without the badminton.

When Ishita was posted as the veterinary officer in a small town in Kangra, her evenings were long and silent. Then Seema, the schoolteacher who lived downstairs, mentioned she played badminton on the school court every Wednesday. "Come if you like."
Ishita went. She was terrible. She went again the next Wednesday, and the next.
It never became a grand friendship overnight. It was forty minutes of shuttles, then tea from Seema's flask on the school steps. Seema complained about exam duty; Ishita told stories about stubborn buffaloes. In November Seema brought extra rajma. In January Ishita drove her to the district hospital when her father fell ill.
By spring, Wednesday was the fixed point of the week. Ishita had other acquaintances in town now, people she nodded to at the market. But it was Seema she called when a landslide blocked the road home.

qa.q: What day do Ishita and Seema play badminton?
qa.a: Every Wednesday.

qa.a: She feels trust and warmth toward Seema, a real bond grown from weeks of steady, modest contact.

qa.q: What made this friendship grow?
qa.a: Regular, modest contact, badminton and tea every Wednesday, which built trust step by step.

qa.q: What might Seema value in this friendship?
qa.a: Seema has someone to share tea and complaints with, and someone who drove her to hospital when her father fell ill.

grounding: In a small town, a weekly badminton game and tea slowly grow into one dependable friendship that matters more than many acquaintances.

When Clara moved into the old building in Prague, she knew nobody. The notice board in the hallway listed a watering rota for the courtyard garden, and the landlady had added her name: Tuesdays, with Ivan from flat 4.
The first Tuesday they watered the tomatoes in silence. The second, Ivan pointed out that snails were eating the lettuce. The third, Clara brought coffee in two mismatched mugs.
Over the summer Tuesdays became their standing appointment. Ivan, a retired tram driver, taught her the Czech names of every herb. Clara helped him set up video calls with his granddaughter in Canada. On bad days at work, she found herself wishing Tuesday would come sooner.
By autumn she knew two other neighbours well enough to borrow sugar. But Ivan was the one she brought soup to when he caught a cold. One steady friend, she thought, was worth a hundred likes.

qa.q: What was Ivan's job before he retired?
qa.a: A tram driver.

qa.q: What does Clara wishing Tuesday would come sooner reveal?
qa.a: She feels comforted and connected, the steady routine with Ivan having become a real friendship.

qa.q: Why did the watering rota help Clara build a real tie?
qa.a: It gave regular, modest contact around a shared chore, letting trust grow slowly over the summer.

qa.q: What might the Tuesday routine mean to Ivan?
qa.a: Ivan gains company, help with calls to his granddaughter, and someone who brings soup when he is ill.

grounding: A shared weekly chore grows into a steady friendship for a young woman new to a city, one bond that counts more than many casual ones.

In the nurses' changing room at the district hospital in Gangtok, Sharmila used to leave after night shift without speaking to anyone. Then Dolma, from the children's ward, asked if she wanted to walk down the hill together on Thursdays after handover, since they both finished at seven.
They did. Every Thursday, twenty minutes down the steep road, past the prayer flags and the momo stall just opening. At first they talked about patients. Then about Dolma's grandmother, Sharmila's cranky landlord, a series they were both watching.
Six months on, Sharmila had a small circle: Dolma, a pharmacist named Karma who sometimes joined them, and the stall owner who kept two plates ready. When Sharmila's mother fell ill back in Siliguri, it was Dolma who swapped a shift without being asked.
She didn't have many friends. She had a few she could count on. That turned out to be enough.

qa.q: What time did Sharmila and Dolma finish their night shifts?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel about her small circle six months on?
qa.a: Sharmila feels settled and supported, content with a few friends she can count on.

qa.q: What built these ties?
qa.a: A regular Thursday walk after the shift, modest and consistent, that slowly deepened into trust.

qa.q: What might Dolma feel swapping a shift for Sharmila?
qa.a: Dolma likely feels caring and glad to help a friend she has come to know well.

grounding: A weekly walk after night shift slowly turns two nurses into close friends, a few steady bonds mattering more than many casual ones.

Dear Nandini Akka,
You asked last month if I'd made any friends here in Hyderabad yet. Honestly, when you asked, not really. But something slowly happened.
Every Saturday at seven, the same four of us play badminton at the colony court. I only went because the watchman kept inviting me. Nobody talked much at first. Now after the game we sit on the wall and argue about whose smash was weaker.
On Wednesdays, Imran from the flat below and I cook together, because neither of us can finish a whole pot of sambar alone. Last week he told me about his father's surgery, and I told him about Appa.
It isn't a big group, Akka. Just three or four people I see every week. But when I had fever last month, two of them brought food. I didn't have that a year ago.
Your brother,
Kishore

qa.q: On which day do Kishore and Imran cook together?
qa.a: They cook together on Wednesdays.

qa.q: How does Kishore seem to feel about the new friendships?
qa.a: Kishore feels grateful and a little surprised, quietly proud that these weekly habits turned into real care when the fever came.

qa.q: What made these ties grow, and what could Kishore keep doing?
qa.a: Showing up every week for badminton and the Wednesday cooking let trust build slowly; keeping those routines steady will keep the friendships growing.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Nandini will probably feel relieved and happy that her brother is no longer alone in Hyderabad.

grounding: Shows regular, modest contact such as a weekly game and shared cooking growing into a few real friendships.
